newsitem.title: UK: Consumer sectors lead growth in construction.
newsitem.headline: Consumer sectors lead growth in construction.

text.p: UK construction is poised for a period of solid growth in the years ahead, with total construction output set to rise by three percent in 1997, four percent in 1998 and 2.5 percent in 1999, a survey said on Friday.

The latest forecast from the Building Materials Producers (BMP) group said the outlook for the industry was brighter than it had for many years because of the booming consumer-related sectors in commercial property and housing.

Charles Novotny, BMP's forecast panel chairman, said: "The sustained growth forecast for construction output will provide a welcome boost for an industry that spent much of the 1990s in recession, will increase employment and will provide the necessary environment to support investment and training."
He said private housing and commercial development would be among the fastest growing sectors and reflected the wider picture of a strong consumer economy.

The sluggish public sector is also expected to be boosted by recent provisions in the July 2 budget to release 900 million stg of capital receipts from the sale of council houses. The cash will be spent on social housing this year and next.
Another factor which should inject some bounce into the public sector is the new Labour government's go-ahead for a string of private finance initiative (PFI) hospital projects.
But BMP warned that the possibility of higher UK interest rates ahead, to curb inflationary pressures, plus the strong pound, could impact on manufacturing investment by exporting companies.
BMP sees interests rates going to 8.5 percent by the middle of next year.

Looking at a sectoral breakdown of BMP's forecasts, in UK housing 1997 is expected to see construction output rise to 7.5 percent -- swinging from a 3.7 percent decline in 1996. In 1998 total housing output is seen at three percent , falling back to one percent in 1999.

This fallback is attributed to the effect of much work being completed as well as higher interest rates damping back economic growth. Most of the growth in this sector is led by the private sector market.

Other new work, which embraces infrastructure, industrial and commercial sectors, is seen showing total output of four percent in 1997 and 1998, versus 0.1 percent in 1996. Output growth is seen slowing in 1999 to three percent.

In the repair and maintenance sector, the total output for 1997 is seen slowing to two percent from 2.6 percent in 1996. But in 1998 it is seen growing to 3.5 percent before declining to two percent in 1999.
